title: Practice: how greedy, ε-greedy and UCB choose
note: Two rounds of three problems. Round 2 matches round 1 idea by idea (greedy locking in, ε-greedy's random picks, UCB's score), in new settings, so a correction in round 1 can carry over to round 2. Answers and worked solutions stay on the server and are shown on the results page after the final test. Each solution step lists the facts it relies on, and `needs` lists the facts without which the answer can't be reached: in the recursive condition Kai can only be right when its notebook holds all of them, correctly explained. The final test uses other settings (banner ads, coffee machines, a study app, podcasts).

items.title: Greedy gets stuck
items.prompt: Three food trucks really average 6, 4 and 1 points per lunch (A, B and C), but you don't know that. On days 1 to 3 you try each once: A happens to serve a bad lunch (2 points), B gives 5 and C gives 1. From day 4 on you follow greedy. Where do you eat on day 50, and why?
options: At A: by day 50 greedy has noticed that A is the best truck
At a different truck each day, because greedy rotates between them
At C, because it has the most room to improve
At B: A's single bad lunch keeps A's average at 2, and greedy never goes back to A to find out

steps.text: After day 3 the averages are A = 2, B = 5 and C = 1, so greedy picks B.
B keeps averaging about 4, well above A's 2. Greedy only ever picks the best average so far, so it never tries A again, and A's average can't change.
One unlucky first lunch hid the best truck for good: on day 50 you still eat at B.

items.title: An explore day
items.prompt: You now choose between three food trucks with ε-greedy, ε = 0.1, and today is an explore day. Your averages so far: A 5.5 (tried 20 times), B 4.0 (18 times) and C 1.2 (15 times). Where can you end up eating today, and why?
options: Only at B or C: exploring means leaving your favourite
Only at C, the truck you have tried least
At any of A, B or C, each equally likely: the random pick ignores the averages
Most likely at A, because exploring still prefers trucks with good averages

steps.text: On an explore day ε-greedy picks a truck at random instead of the best average.
The random pick ignores the averages and how often each truck was tried: A, B and C each have a 1 in 3 chance, your favourite A included, and C too, although it is known to be bad.
Going to the truck tried least would be closer to what UCB does; ε-greedy doesn't look at the counts.

items.title: Which truck does UCB pick?
items.prompt: Now you choose between the three trucks with UCB. Today truck A has average 6.1 (tried 30 times, UCB bonus 0.5), B has average 4.8 (tried twice, bonus 1.9) and C has average 5.5 (tried 12 times, bonus 0.8). Where does UCB send you, and why?
options: To A, because it has the best average
To B, because its average plus its bonus is the highest
To C, because it has been tried neither too often nor too rarely
To a random truck, because UCB explores at random on some days

steps.text: Add each bonus to the average: A = 6.6, B = 6.7, C = 6.3.
UCB picks the highest score: B. Its average is the lowest, but two lunches say little, so B gets the benefit of the doubt.
Nothing here is random: with the same history UCB always picks the same truck.

items.title: Greedy and the headlines
items.prompt: A news site tests three headlines with greedy. Their true click rates are 0.30 (A), 0.20 (B) and 0.05 (C), but the site doesn't know that. Each headline is shown once first: A gets no click, B gets a click and C gets no click. From then on the site follows greedy. Which headline is it showing after 10,000 visitors, and why?
options: B: A's average stayed at 0 after one missed click, and greedy never shows A again to find out
A: by then greedy has found out that A gets the most clicks
All three in turn, because greedy rotates between them
C, because it has been shown the least

steps.text: After the first three visitors the averages are A = 0, B = 1 and C = 0, so greedy shows B.
B's average settles near 0.20 but can't fall to 0 after its first click, while A and C stay at 0 because greedy never shows them again.
So the site shows B forever, although A has the best click rate: one unlucky first visitor hid it.

items.title: How often ε-greedy shows its favourite
items.prompt: The site switches to ε-greedy with ε = 0.2 on the same three headlines. Headline A has the best average and stays the favourite. About how many of the next 1,000 visitors see headline A?

steps.text: With probability 1 − ε = 0.8 the site exploits and shows its favourite: 800 of the 1,000 visitors see A directly.
The other 200 visitors get one of the three headlines at random, A included, so about a third of them, 67, see A too.
In total about 800 + 67 = 867 visitors see A.

items.title: After B has been tried more
items.prompt: UCB plays four slot machines. Machine B had been played only 3 times, so its bonus was large and UCB played it next. After 20 more plays of B, its average has settled at 4.0 and its bonus has shrunk to 0.6. The other machines' UCB scores are about the same as before: A 5.4, C 3.8 and D 5.1. What does UCB do next, and why?
options: It keeps playing B, because B was picked last time
It plays C, because C has the lowest score and needs more tries
It plays A: every play of B shrank B's bonus, so B's score (4.6) fell below A's
It picks a machine at random, to explore

steps.text: Each play of B made its bonus smaller. Its score fell below A's 5.4 (and D's 5.1), so UCB plays A, the highest score.
UCB moved on without any random pick: it only keeps exploring an option while the bonus keeps its score on top.
